In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular basis of a genetic disorder of insulin secretion, persistent hyperinsulinism hypoglycemic of infancy (PHH).
understanding the structure-function relationship of the sulfonyurea receptor 2 and the role of mutations in the sulphonylurea receptor in the pathogenesis of persistent hyperinsulinism of infancy.
the molecular basis of the K(ATp) channel in pancreatic islets and the pathogenesis of persistent hyperinsulinism of infancy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the KATP channel dysfunction is a common feature of all PHHI mutations, including the novel mutations reported here.
the mutations in the SUR1 gene that we have studied are all loss-of-function mutations that result in the generation of channels with reduced ATP sensitivity and reduced sensitivity to MgADPR.
mutations in SUR1 associated with PHHI are not only distributed throughout the protein, but also have varied effects on channel function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the K(ATP)-channel is the target of the sulfonyureas and the potassium channel opener, diazoxide.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the SUR1 mutations associated with PHHI have varied effects on channel properties, including channel activity and sensitivity to MgADPi and diazoxide.
mutations in SUR1 are associated with a wide range of functional defects in the KATP channels, and the functional defects are not restricted to the nucleotide-binding folds.
